title: Proposition 319: Photo Enforcement Systems and Voter Approval

context.text: Referred to the ballot by the Arizona Legislature as Senate Concurrent Resolution 1004 (2026), which passed the Senate 16-12 on Feb. 26, 2026 and the House 37-18 on June 12, 2026, per Arizona Legislature floor-vote records.

question.text: PROPOSITION 319. REFERRED TO THE PEOPLE BY THE LEGISLATURE RELATING TO PHOTO ENFORCEMENT SYSTEMS. OFFICIAL TITLE: AMENDING SECTION 28-1201, ARIZONA REVISED STATUTES; AMENDING TITLE 28, CHAPTER 3, ARTICLE 21, ARIZONA REVISED STATUTES, BY ADDING SECTION 28-1207. DESCRIPTIVE TITLE: PROHIBITS STATE AGENCIES AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS FROM USING PHOTO ENFORCEMENT SYSTEMS FOR TRAFFIC ENFORCEMENT UNLESS PROVIDED BY CONTRACT AS OF DECEMBER 31, 2026; REQUIRES LOCAL GOVERNMENTS TO OBTAIN VOTER APPROVAL TO CONTINUE THEIR USE.

summary.text: Prohibits a local authority or state agency from using a photo enforcement system for speeding or traffic-control-device violations unless it has a contract in place before Dec. 31, 2026. A local authority with such a contract would have to seek voter approval at the next general election to continue; if voters decline, it must stop within 90 days, and if they approve, it may operate for 10 years, after which approval must be sought again for each additional 10-year period.

measure.yesMeans: A "yes" vote shall have the effect of: (1) prohibiting state agencies and local governments from using photo enforcement systems to identify violators of traffic laws unless the agency or government contracts to use those systems by December 31, 2026; and (2) requiring local governments to obtain voter approval of existing photo enforcement systems at the next regular general election and every 10 years afterward to continue using photo enforcement systems.
measure.noMeans: A "no" vote shall have the effect of maintaining the current laws governing photo enforcement systems.

argumentsFor.text: Kristin Baumgartner, Prescott: "It bans new automated camera systems and requires cities and towns with existing contracts to obtain voter approval at the ballot box."
Emerson Jones, Phoenix: "Enough is enough: vote YES and stop the government from treating law-abiding citizens like ATM machines."

argumentsAgainst.text: Arizona Public Health Association (Will Humble, Executive Director): "It takes an important safety tool, red-light cameras, away from every city and town in Arizona that doesn't already have them."
AAA Arizona (Michelle Donati, Director, Government Affairs): "Proposition 319 goes too far. It permanently bans photo enforcement for any city without a program running by the end of the year."

currentLaw.text: Per the Arizona Senate fact sheet: the state or a local authority may not use a photo enforcement system on a state highway to identify violators of speed restrictions or traffic signs, signals and markings; a local authority or state agency using one must adopt standards indicating to drivers that a system is present and operational (A.R.S. 28-1204, 28-1206). A person who receives a mailed notice of violation obtained with a photo enforcement system does not have to identify who is in the photo or respond to the notice, though not responding may lead to official service and an additional fee (A.R.S. 28-1602). The House summary notes similar legislation (SB1019) was vetoed by the Governor in the 1st Regular Session.

fiscalImpact.text: Arizona Senate fact sheet: "There is no anticipated fiscal impact to the state General Fund associated with this legislation." The Legislative Council analysis and publicity pamphlet give no fiscal estimate.

opponents.text: Arizona Public Health Association (Executive Director Will Humble).
AAA Arizona (Michelle Donati, Director, Government Affairs).
Institute of Transportation Engineers Arizona Section (Germaine Calimlim, Traffic Engineer).
Civic Engagement Beyond Voting (Co-Directors Melinda Iyer and Catherine Sigmon).

researchNotes: Slate: the Secretary of State's official 2026 General Election Publicity Pamphlet (hosted by the Citizens Clean Elections Commission; azsos.gov itself returned a bot-protection block and was not bypassed) lists exactly eight statewide measures: Propositions 141, 142, 144, 316, 317, 318, 319 and 320. Ballot question, 'yes'/'no' text: copied from the pamphlet's 'Ballot Format' page for this proposition. Arguments: excerpts of arguments published in that pamphlet, attributed to the signer and sponsoring organization it prints; the pamphlet prints many arguments per side (it reproduces spelling and punctuation as submitted), so these are a selection of 2 for and 2 against, not the full set. Legislative vote counts are from the Arizona Legislature's floor-action records. The pamphlet contains no fiscal estimate for this measure. Required vote: a majority of those voting. Enrichment: no campaign-finance totals for committees on this measure were found (Arizona campaign finance portal not retrievable); no organized supporter beyond the bill sponsor was found in the pamphlet, whose 'for' arguments are by individual voters.
